summary: Describes security threats for larger multicast routing infrastructures, within or between domains. It analyzes PIM-SM in its main operational modes, including any-source and source-specific multicast, and suggests enhancements. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4609 describes how attackers can misuse PIM-SM multicast routing to consume router resources or disturb multicast traffic. It compares ASM, SSM, and Embedded-RP and discusses ways to limit attack effects.

subtitle: Threats to multicast routing and ways to limit the damage from forged joins and data.

tldr.problem: PIM Sparse Mode can be abused to create excessive routing state, send data to groups without receivers, or disrupt traffic in existing groups.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes threats in ASM, SSM, and Embedded-RP operation and discusses rate limits, remote-routability checks, and passive PIM operation on stub links.
tldr.outcome: It offers security analysis and possible enhancements, not one protection that addresses every threat. It says SSM resists unwanted source traffic better, while forged joins can still create state.

today: RFC 4609 is an Informational RFC published in August 2006. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it analyzes PIM-SM security threats and possible mitigations.

sections.title: Scope and Multicast Models
sections.content:
The RFC analyzes security threats to multicast routing infrastructures that use Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM). It considers Any-Source Multicast (ASM), Source-Specific Multicast (SSM), and ASM with Embedded-RP.

The focus is on attacks affecting multicast routing infrastructure, not on-link attacks against hosts or end-to-end protection of multicast payloads. The analysis assumes that multicast routers are generally trustworthy.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC focuses on attacks that affect multicast routing infrastructure. It compares three PIM-SM operating models and does not cover attacks limited to one local link.

sections.title: Receiver-Based Join Flooding
sections.content:
A receiver-based attack occurs when a host repeatedly joins different groups or SSM channels, including groups or sources that do not exist. Each join can cause a Designated Router to send a PIM Join and create state along the route.

The RFC says this state lasts 260 seconds by default without further IGMP or MLD reports or leaves. It gives an example of 100 joins per second, each with 10 sources, creating 260,000 state entries after 260 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: A host can ask routers to join many made-up groups. Routers may keep the resulting state for a time even though no multicast source or receiver exists.

sections.title: Source-Based Attacks
sections.content:
Data flooding occurs when a host sends multicast packets to a group without subscribers. The work can consume router processing, and in ASM the source may be announced through MSDP. The RFC says MSDP repeats source-active information every 60 seconds by default while the source remains active.

A group-integrity attack sends unwanted packets into an existing group. SSM prevents other sources from injecting traffic into a channel unless the source address can be spoofed. ASM and Embedded-RP allow sources to send through a rendezvous point, which may forward packets to receivers.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending packets to empty groups wastes router resources. Sending packets to an active group can disturb receivers, especially when the multicast model allows many sources.

sections.title: Differences Among ASM, SSM, and Embedded-RP
sections.content:
The RFC compares the models across forged joins, ability to send as a source, and group integrity. ASM has weak resistance to forged joins and source attacks. SSM is much more resistant to unwanted sources, but forged joins can still create state.

Embedded-RP limits some choices by deriving the rendezvous point from the group address, but forged joins and register attacks remain possible. PIM does not carry receiver identity beyond the directly connected router, so upstream routers cannot use that information to decide which receivers may join.
sections.plainLanguage: SSM gives receivers more control over which source they accept, but it does not stop forged join requests. ASM and Embedded-RP have different source-injection risks.

sections.title: Mitigation Options
sections.content:
The RFC discusses rate limits at several points: group-management reports at the Designated Router, multicast traffic from a source, PIM signaling, register decapsulation at a rendezvous point, and MSDP source-active messages. These can limit state creation or reduce processing load, but may also affect legitimate hosts on the same link.

Remote-routability checks can help avoid maintaining state for an unreachable source or rendezvous point. Passive PIM mode lets hosts receive multicast on a stub link without the router sending or processing PIM packets on that interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Rate limits can reduce the effect of bursts of joins, data, or control messages. Checks for reachable sources and passive operation on stub links offer other forms of protection, each with tradeoffs.

sections.title: Authentication Is Not the Whole Answer
sections.content:
The RFC does not specify new authentication mechanisms. It notes that PIM-SM describes using IPsec for routing authentication and that IGMPv3 also describes IPsec use for group management.

Authentication can help prevent unauthorized control messages, but does not ensure that an authenticated host behaves correctly. Cryptographic processing can also create a denial-of-service target if routers must perform too many operations.
sections.plainLanguage: Authentication can help verify control messages, but an authenticated host may still behave badly. The RFC also warns that cryptographic checks consume router resources.
